reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard rheumatology references
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive autoinflammatory disorder caused by partial deficiency of mevalonate kinase due to MVK gene mutations
Attacks typically begin in infancy and are frequently precipitated by vaccinations, minor infections, or stress
Febrile episodes last several days and are accompanied by tender cervical lymphadenopathy, abdominal pain, vomiting or diarrhoea, and arthralgia
Mucocutaneous features such as aphthous ulcers and a variable rash are common
Many but not all patients have persistently elevated serum IgD, so a normal IgD does not exclude the diagnosis
During attacks, urinary mevalonic acid excretion is increased, and enzyme assay or MVK genetic testing confirms the diagnosis
Complete rather than partial loss of mevalonate kinase activity produces the severe systemic phenotype mevalonic aciduria with neurological involvement
IL-1 inhibition is the mainstay of treatment for reducing attack frequency and severity
reference.pathophysiology: Reduced activity of mevalonate kinase impairs the isoprenoid/cholesterol biosynthetic pathway downstream of mevalonate. Deficient production of nonsterol isoprenoids, particularly geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate needed for protein prenylation, leads to dysregulated inflammasome activity and excessive interleukin-1 beta release, driving recurrent systemic inflammation. Temperature sensitivity of the mutant enzyme partly explains fever-triggered flares.
additionalDifferentials: Other hereditary periodic fever syndromes (FMF, TRAPS, CAPS)
additionalInvestigations: MVK genetic testing and/or mevalonate kinase enzyme activity assay
Urinary mevalonic acid during an attack
Serum IgD (and often IgA), recognising normal levels do not exclude the disease
Acute-phase reactants during and between episodes
redFlags: Neurological impairment, failure to thrive, or dysmorphism suggesting the severe mevalonic aciduria phenotype
Frequent disabling attacks impairing growth and development in children
Proteinuria indicating the rare occurrence of secondary AA amyloidosis
Severe abdominal symptoms requiring exclusion of a surgical cause
reference.prognosis: The partial-deficiency (HIDS) phenotype tends to improve in frequency with age and responds well to IL-1 blockade, with generally preserved life expectancy; the complete-deficiency mevalonic aciduria form carries a much poorer outlook with neurological damage and early mortality.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis on the basis of a normal serum IgD
Missing the vaccination-triggered pattern of attacks in young children
Failing to distinguish partial deficiency from severe mevalonic aciduria
Attributing recurrent fevers with lymphadenopathy solely to intercurrent infections
